messages.subject: About the implementation of a Point-quarter method and a random
messages.subject_clean: About the implementation of a Point-quarter method and a random
messages.body_plain:
Hello:

Your opinion is requested for this case.

I want to estimate the density of a columnar cactus in Mexico.  I plan
to use the point-quarter method.

A) Suppose I stratify the population in these height classes:

0.2 to < 1.0 m
1.0 to < 3.0 m
3.0 m to infinite

My goal is to get an accurate estimation of the absolute density for
each stratum and the frequency or proportion of individuals in each
stratum.

B) Suppose I use THE SAME random point for measuring the distance to the
nearest four (pooled) individuals in the stratum 1 and 2, AND for
measuring the distance to the four individuals in the stratum 3, i.e. I
would sample the densities for two stocks (stratum 1 and 2, and stratum
3) BUT USING THE SAME random points.

C) I plan to put the random points in a random walk procedure, i.e.,
from an arbitrary original point I will find the first point according a
random distance (0, 1, 2, 3, ... 30 m, i.e. each meter in the interval
0-30 m) and a random azimuth (0, 1, 2, 3, ... 357, 358, 359 degrees,
i.e., each degree in the interval 0-359 degrees).  After making the
first point, from this new position, I would repeat the procedure for
the second point, etc.

D) An alternative procedure could be measure distances from the random
point to the four nearest individuals regardless their height, i.e. ONLY
ONE sampling for the pooled strata.  The density for each stratum would
be calculated by means of:

Overall density x frequency of individuals in each stratum

and

frequency = individuals in one stratum / total number of individuals in
the sampling

"Individuals in one stratum" and "total number of individuals in the
sampling" mean individuals to which distances to a random point are
measured.

E) In relation to point A, this procedure I would apply for estimate the
densities for individuals in the strata 1 and 2, based in the overall
density of individuals from 0.2 to < 3.0 m, i.e. pooled classes 1 and
2).

What you think about the combined procedures B) and E) or, in general,
procedure B) vs. procedure D)?  What do you think about procedure C) for
establishing the random points?

Thanks for all, and excuse my English and the length of my text.

Fernando Vite

From: Steve Buckland <st...@mcs.st-andrews.ac.uk>
To: Fernando Vite <vi...@xanum.uam.mx>
Subject: Re: About the implementation of a Point-quarter method and a
    random walk procedure for establishing the sampling points.

Fernando, I would not use that approach at all.  It is a very inefficient
way to estimate absolute density.  Random walk does not give you a
representative sample to estimate density.  You need to define the area
for which you require density estimates, then take a random/representative
sample of points or lines within that area.  Lines (line or strip transect
sampling) is likely to be far more efficient than points.

I suggest you read one of our books on this subject before implementing a
design.  The disadvantages of your proposed approach are spelt out on p294
of our 1993 book, which is available free on our web pages.  The 2001 book
would be better (see our web pages for how to get it), as it addresses
survey design issues in much greater detail than the 1993 book (chapter
7).  Point-to-nearest-object methods are summarized in pp223-5 of that
book.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: flocks of birds, independent observations, longspurs and sparrows
messages.subject_clean: flocks of birds, independent observations, longspurs and sparrows
messages.body_plain:
I would like to ask your help with a sampling problem I have.

I am studying sampling methods for wintering grassland birds. My methods are
line transects, point counts, and area searches in which I delineate an area
and try to flush all birds. I will analyze the line transect and point count
data using DISTANCE.

My problem is that different species flock differently. All birds I study
are found in the grass and almost always detected by flushing. Longspurs
form large flocks (up to 200), Savannah Sparrows can be found individually
or in small flocks (up to 10), and LeConte's Sparrows are almost always alone.

I want estimate density for each species. My question is how to group
observations. A "typical" observation of a Longspur flock will start with a
few individuals flushing. Walking a few meters further will flush more, then
more, then there will be an explosion of sometimes hundreds of birds.
Walking a few meters more will often flush even more scattered individuals.
It is unlikely that these  birds represent independent samples, as they all
group together and fly around and around overhead, with subsequently flushed
birds gradually joining the previously flushed birds in one large flock
overhead. Then the whole group will usually go and alight somewhere else.
The flock will sometimes be spread over nearly 0.5ha of ground.
- What should constitute one "observation" of these birds? The entire flock?
Each flushed "sub-group" of the flock? I am thinking the entire group should
be recorded as one observation, but to what extent should I include
scattered individuals and groups in the main flock?

Savannah Sparrows pose a different problem. They form very loose flocks,
often of two to five individuals scattered over 100 m. Individual
observations I can record as one, but often two or more individuals with
nearly 100m of distance between them will, when one is flushed, draw nearer
to each other and begin to behave as a flock. The other members of the flock
may be detected when they flush, or may be picked up flying toward the
flushed individual as all draw tighter together. Often one individual is
flushed, then flies, and "picks up" another individual as it  flies and they
both go off together. Another situation is when one bird flushes, flies a
few meters down the transect, then when I flush it again there are several
more birds with it. It obviously flew to where its comrades were.
- Any advice on how to handle these observations? These birds do not seem to
be behaving independently, even when they have considerable distance between
them.

I apologize for the length of this, but I wanted to give enough details. I
would appreciate any help you can give.

Sincerely,
Joe Roberts
Graduate Student
Univ. of Oklahoma

messages.subject: Re: flocks of birds, independent observations,
messages.body_plain:
Joe, the methods in Distance are very robust to non-independence,
especially if you select the bootstrap for estimating variance.  For the
longspurs, I would definitely treat the sub-groups as the
units.  Otherwise you can get considerable bias because location of the
group tends to be recorded too close to the line on average.  You can
expect poor precision for species that behave like this, because encounter
rate is so variable between lines.

For savannah sparrows, I would treat each individual as a separate
sighting.  Record their position as the location from which they fly
up.  If you're not sure where they came from, don't record them - this
doesn't cause a problem except when they were actually very close to the
line, in which case g(0) may be less than one, so try to monitor near the
line so that such birds are likely to be detected as they fly.  There is
another more subtle issue with 'chain flushes'.  This tends to increase
the effective width of your search strip in areas where density is higher,
leading to overestimation of the effective strip width, and a tendency to
underestimate density as a consequence.  The effect can be reduced by
truncating distances from the line more severely than would normally be
the case.

Steve Buckland

messages.subject: CDS versus MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Dear List
I have conducted a stratified line transect survey . I have modeled the detection function using two approaches CDS and MCDS. I used habitat vegetation type and terrain type as covariates. I used categoial scale to evaluate both variables. The density estimates coming out of the two approaches ( using global detection function ) were very similar . I had a density estimate of 184.414 with CV of 35.34% following MCDS and 183.09 with CV of 35.47% following CDS. I conducted a AIC test for the two conditions using the same truncation point and same interval cut points. I had the following results:
CDS- Half normal model  : AIC= 457.747
MCDS- Half normal model : AIC= 459.890.
I know that I should go for the model that results in lower AIC. My question is :
Should I go for the use of covariates in modeling the detection function although it has a higher AIC because I think that variability in vegetation and terrain types are definitely affecting the observer detectability?  OR should I just apply what the statistical test implies of the CDS being a better model?

I find it hard to reject the MCDS especially with Density estimates being so similar as point estimates and associated CV.

Hope to find some opinion to help.
Husam El Alqamy

messages.subject: Re: CDS versus MCDS
messages.body_plain:
Hi Husam, list,

AIC attempts to trade off reducing bias by adding more parameters vs increasing
variance and model complexity (see the Distance book 3.4.2 and references there
for more on this).  The formula is AIC= -2logL + 2q, where L is the likelihood
and q is the number of parameters.  We can interpret the first part -2logL as a
measure of how well the model fits the data, and the second part as a penalty
for addition of parameters.  In your case, adding the two factor covariates has
improved model fit (reduced -2logL), but not enough to overcome the penalty 2q
of adding the extra parameters.  So, you get the "best" estimate of global
density (in terms of the trade-off between bias and variance) by not including
the covariates.  Although you know the covariates have an effect, it appears to
be too weak, given the amount of data you have, to justify putting them in the
model.

Of course AIC is not a panacea; there are plenty of times that I ignore AIC
altogether in analyses -- for example when there are problems in the data such
as evasive movement.  Also it's important to look at goodness-of-fit as well as
AIC.

One time you would definitely want to consider the MCDS fit is when you are
going to estimate density by vegetation and terrain type, rather than globally.
In that case, using the global detection function will result in biased
estimates by vegetation and terrain type.  If there is enough data, try
stratifying by vegetation and terrain type, and compare the AIC of this analysis
with one where vegetation and terrain type are covariates.  Use the analysis
with the lower AIC.

Cheers,

 - Len

--

messages.subject: Announcement: Distance Workshops September 2003, Scotland
messages.body_plain:
**********************************************************
ANNOUNCEMENT
**********************************************************

DISTANCE WORKSHOPS 2003
St Andrews, Fife, Scotland

**********************************************************

The Centre for Research into Ecological and Environmental Modelling
(CREEM) is hosting another set of Distance Sampling workshops in
September of this year. The aim of these workshops is to train
participants in the latest methods for design and analysis of
distance sampling surveys, including line and point transects. The
workshops are taught by leading researchers in the field, using
Distance software.

*********************************************************

Workshop 1: Introduction to Distance Sampling, 10-12 September
An introductory workshop focusing on standard distance sampling
methods. The workshop will be a blend of theory and practice and
participants will learn how to use version 4 of the program Distance.
Participants will gain a solid grounding in both survey design and
methods of analysis for distance sampling surveys.

**********************************************************

Workshop 2: Advanced Techniques and Recent Developments in Distance
Sampling,
15-17 September
A workshop designed for those who are already familiar with the
basics, where we will teach advanced material such as automated
survey design, adaptive sampling, incorporating covariates into the
detection function, methods for where g(0)<1, and spatial modelling
of density. Participants will learn the more advanced features of
version 4 of Distance.

**********************************************************

For both workshops, participants are encouraged to bring their own
data sets, and can expect to do some preliminary analyses of their
data.

The number of participants on both workshops is strictly limited, and
for this reason we encourage you to register as soon as possible.
Information and forms can be downloaded from our web site,
www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/conferences.php <http://www.creem.st-and.ac.uk/conferences.php>
